anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: How is the abdomen divided into nine regions?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: By two vertical (midclavicular) planes and two horizontal planes (the subcostal & transtubercular).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Name the nine abdominal regions.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: Top: right hypochondrium, epigastrium, left hypochondrium; middle: right lumbar, umbilical, left lumbar; bottom: right iliac, hypogastrium, left iliac.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What structures lie in the transpyloric plane (L1)?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The pylorus, fundus of the gallbladder, neck of the pancreas, origin of the SMA, and the hila of the kidneys — midway between the xiphisternum and umbilicus.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Where is McBurney's point, and what does it overlie?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: One-third of the way from the ASIS to the umbilicus — the surface marking of the base of the appendix.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Name the two layers of superficial fascia below the umbilicus.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: Camper’s fascia (fatty, superficial) and Scarpa’s fascia (membranous, deep).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: List the layers of the anterior abdominal wall from superficial to deep.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: Skin → Camper’s & Scarpa’s fascia → muscles → transversalis fascia → extraperitoneal fat → parietal peritoneum.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What is Scarpa's fascia continuous with, and why does it matter?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: With Colles’ fascia in the perineum and the dartos of the scrotum/penis — explaining how extravasated urine tracks into the scrotum & abdominal wall.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Give the fibre directions of the three flat abdominal muscles.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: External oblique — inferomedial (“hands in pockets”); internal oblique — superomedial; transversus abdominis — transverse.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What is the linea alba, and the linea semilunaris?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The linea alba is the midline fusion of the aponeuroses; the linea semilunaris is the curved lateral border of rectus abdominis.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What is the innervation of the anterior abdominal wall muscles?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The anterior rami of T7–T12 (& L1) — the thoraco-abdominal (and subcostal/iliohypogastric/ilioinguinal) nerves.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Describe the rectus sheath ABOVE the arcuate line.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The internal oblique aponeurosis splits: anterior wall = EO + anterior IO lamina; posterior wall = posterior IO lamina + transversus abdominis.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Describe the rectus sheath BELOW the arcuate line.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: All three aponeuroses pass anterior to rectus abdominis, so the posterior wall is only transversalis fascia (a weak point).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Where is the arcuate line?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: About one-third of the way from the umbilicus to the pubic symphysis — the lower limit of the posterior rectus sheath aponeurosis.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What is the inguinal ligament and its attachments?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The rolled-under lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis, running from the ASIS to the pubic tubercle.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Where are the deep and superficial inguinal rings?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The deep ring is a defect in the transversalis fascia, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; the superficial ring is a triangular defect in the external oblique aponeurosis.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What forms the walls of the inguinal canal?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: Anterior: EO aponeurosis (+ IO laterally); posterior: transversalis fascia (+ conjoint tendon medially); roof: arching IO & TA fibres; floor: inguinal ligament (+ lacunar ligament).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What are the contents of the inguinal canal?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The spermatic cord (♂) or round ligament of the uterus (♀), plus the ilioinguinal nerve (which lies on the cord, not within it).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: List the three arteries of the spermatic cord.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The testicular artery, the cremasteric artery, and the artery to the vas (ductus) deferens.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: List the nerves associated with the spermatic cord.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (which is itself the nerve to cremaster) and sympathetic (autonomic) fibres; the ilioinguinal nerve runs on the cord (not within its coverings) — together these make up the traditional “three nerves.”

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: List the three 'other' contents of the spermatic cord.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The vas (ductus) deferens, the pampiniform plexus of veins, and lymphatics.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Name the three coverings of the spermatic cord and their origins.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: External spermatic fascia (from external oblique), cremasteric fascia (from internal oblique), internal spermatic fascia (from transversalis fascia).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What are the boundaries of Hesselbach's (inguinal) triangle?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: Medial — lateral border of rectus abdominis; lateral — inferior epigastric vessels; inferior — inguinal ligament.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Distinguish an indirect from a direct inguinal hernia.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: Indirect — through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; congenital (patent processus vaginalis); may reach the scrotum. Direct — through Hesselbach’s triangle, medial to the vessels; acquired (weak wall).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: How do you clinically distinguish an inguinal from a femoral hernia?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: A hernia above & medial to the pubic tubercle is inguinal; one below & lateral to the pubic tubercle is femoral.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: How can pressure over the deep ring differentiate hernia types?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: After reduction, pressure over the deep ring (just above the mid-inguinal point / femoral pulse) controls an indirect hernia; a direct hernia still bulges.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Name the muscles of the posterior abdominal wall.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: Psoas major, quadratus lumborum, iliacus (and transversus abdominis laterally).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What is iliopsoas, and its main action?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: Psoas major + iliacus, inserting on the lesser trochanter — the chief flexor of the hip.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Name the three folds on the internal surface of the anterior abdominal wall.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The median umbilical fold (urachus), the medial umbilical folds (obliterated umbilical arteries), and the lateral umbilical folds (inferior epigastric vessels).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What is a rectus sheath haematoma?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: Bleeding from torn inferior epigastric vessels (typically below the arcuate line) → a painful abdominal wall mass that can mimic an acute abdomen.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What dermatome is the umbilicus, and its clinical relevance?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: T10 — early appendicitis pain is referred here (peri-umbilical) before localising to the right iliac fossa.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Distinguish parietal from visceral peritoneum in terms of pain.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: Parietal peritoneum has somatic innervation → sharp, well-localised pain; visceral peritoneum has autonomic innervation → dull, poorly localised, midline-referred pain.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: What connects the greater and lesser sacs?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: The epiploic (omental) foramen of Winslow.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: List the retroperitoneal structures (SAD PUCKER).
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: Suprarenals, Aorta/IVC, Duodenum (2nd–4th), Pancreas (except tail), Ureters, Colon (ascending & descending), Kidneys, oEsophagus, Rectum.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Give the artery, vertebral level and referred pain for the FOREGUT.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: Coeliac trunk (T12); pain referred to the epigastrium. Foregut = oesophagus → mid-duodenum + liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Give the artery, level and referred pain for the MIDGUT.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: Superior mesenteric artery (SMA, L1); pain referred to the periumbilical region. Midgut = mid-duodenum → proximal ⅔ of the transverse colon.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Give the artery, level and referred pain for the HINDGUT.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: Inferior mesenteric artery (IMA, L3); pain referred to the suprapubic region. Hindgut = distal ⅓ transverse colon → the upper anal canal (down to the pectinate line).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Where is the foregut–midgut boundary?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: At the 2nd part of the duodenum, at the major duodenal papilla (of Vater).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Name the regions of the stomach.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: The cardia, fundus, body, pyloric antrum & pylorus.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Describe the arterial supply of the stomach.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: Lesser curve: left gastric (coeliac) + right gastric (hepatic); greater curve: left gastro-omental (splenic) + right gastro-omental (gastroduodenal); fundus: short gastric arteries (splenic).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Name the four parts of the duodenum and a key feature of each.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: 1st (superior) — the cap, common ulcer site; 2nd (descending) — major duodenal papilla; 3rd (horizontal) — crossed by SMA/SMV; 4th (ascending) — ends at the duodenojejunal flexure (ligament of Treitz).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Contrast the jejunum and ileum.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: Jejunum (upper left) — thick wall, tall plicae circulares, long vasa recta, few arcades; ileum (lower right) — thin wall, Peyer’s patches, short vasa recta, many arcades.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: State Meckel's diverticulum 'rule of 2s'.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: 2% of people, 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve, 2 inches long, 2 tissue types (may contain gastric/pancreatic mucosa).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: How is the large intestine distinguished from the small?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: By teniae coli (3 longitudinal muscle bands), haustra (sacculations), omental appendices (fat tags) and a wider calibre.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Where do the teniae coli converge, and what is the commonest appendix position?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: They converge on the base of the appendix (a surgical guide); the commonest position is retrocaecal.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Give the SMA branches to the colon.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: Ileocolic, right colic & middle colic arteries (to the proximal ⅔ of the transverse colon).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Give the IMA branches to the colon.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: Left colic, sigmoid & superior rectal arteries.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: What is the marginal artery of Drummond, and the watershed area?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: An anastomotic channel along the colon linking the SMA & IMA; the splenic flexure is a watershed vulnerable to ischaemia.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Name the four anatomical lobes of the liver.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: The right, left, caudate & quadrate lobes (functionally divided into 8 Couinaud segments by the vessels).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: What structures form the portal triad in the porta hepatis?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: The portal vein, hepatic artery & common hepatic (bile) duct.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: What does the ligamentum teres represent, and where does it run?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: The obliterated left umbilical vein, running in the free edge of the falciform ligament.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Trace the extrahepatic biliary tree.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: Right + left hepatic ducts → common hepatic duct; joined by the cystic duct → common bile duct → joins the main pancreatic duct at the ampulla of Vater (sphincter of Oddi).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: What are the boundaries and contents of Calot's triangle?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: The cystic duct, common hepatic duct & inferior edge of the liver; it contains the cystic artery — the key landmark in cholecystectomy.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Describe the parts and relations of the pancreas.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: Head (in the duodenal C, with the uncinate process), neck, body & tail (to the splenic hilum); retroperitoneal except the tail; the SMA/SMV pass behind the neck.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Where does the spleen lie, and along which ribs?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: In the left hypochondrium, along ribs 9–11; intraperitoneal, the largest lymphoid organ.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Which structures form the renal hilum from front to back?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: The renal Vein, Artery & ureter (renal pelvis) — “VAU” anterior to posterior.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Which kidney is lower, and why?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: The right kidney is lower, displaced by the liver.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Trace the flow of urine within the kidney.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: Collecting ducts → renal papilla → minor calyx → major calyx → renal pelvis → ureter.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Describe the course and constrictions of the ureter.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: It runs on psoas major, crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery at the pelvic brim, then down the pelvic wall to the bladder; constrictions at the PUJ, pelvic brim & VUJ.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Describe the adrenal (suprarenal) glands and their venous drainage.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: Retroperitoneal caps on each kidney with a cortex (glomerulosa/fasciculata/reticularis) & medulla; a rich 3-source arterial supply but a single vein — right → IVC, left → left renal vein.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.front: Which artery lies behind the first part of the duodenum, and its clinical relevance?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.back: The gastroduodenal artery — a posterior D1 (duodenal) ulcer can erode it, causing brisk upper-GI haemorrhage.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: From which roots is the lumbar plexus formed, and where does it lie?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: The anterior rami of L1–L4 (+ a twig from T12), within the psoas major muscle.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Give the mnemonic for the lumbar plexus branches.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: “I, I, Get, Leftovers, On, Fridays”: Iliohypogastric, Ilioinguinal, Genitofemoral, Lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh, Obturator, Femoral.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Which lumbar plexus nerves emerge from the lateral, anterior and medial aspects of psoas?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Lateral border — femoral & lateral cutaneous nerves; anterior surface — genitofemoral; medial border — obturator.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What are the roots and territory of the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Both L1: they supply the lower abdominal wall; the ilioinguinal also supplies the upper medial thigh & anterior scrotum/labium (running through the inguinal canal).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What does the genitofemoral nerve (L1–L2) supply?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Its genital branch → the cremaster muscle (& anterior scrotum); its femoral branch → skin over the femoral triangle.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What are the roots of the femoral and obturator nerves?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Both L2–L4: the femoral supplies the anterior thigh (quadriceps); the obturator supplies the medial thigh (adductors).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What is the lumbosacral trunk?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Fibres from L4–L5 that descend into the pelvis to join the sacral plexus, linking the lumbar and sacral plexuses.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What is special about the splanchnic nerves' path through the sympathetic chain?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: They are preganglionic sympathetic fibres that pass through the chain without synapsing, synapsing instead in the pre-aortic (prevertebral) ganglia.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Give the roots, ganglion and target of the GREATER splanchnic nerve.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: T5–T9 → the coeliac ganglion → the foregut.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Give the roots, ganglion and target of the LESSER splanchnic nerve.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: T10–T11 → the aorticorenal / superior mesenteric ganglion → the midgut.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Give the roots and target of the LEAST splanchnic nerve.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: T12 → the renal plexus (kidney).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What do the lumbar splanchnic nerves supply?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: L1–L2 preganglionic sympathetics → the inferior mesenteric / superior hypogastric plexuses → the hindgut & pelvis.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What are the effects of SYMPATHETIC stimulation on the gut?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: ↓ motility & secretion, contracts sphincters and vasoconstriction (diverts blood away from digestion).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What are the parasympathetic supplies to the gut, and their territories?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: The vagus (CN X) supplies the foregut & midgut (to the distal ⅓ of the transverse colon); the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–4) supply the hindgut.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What are the effects of PARASYMPATHETIC stimulation on the gut?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: ↑ motility & secretion and relaxation of sphincters (“rest & digest”).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Where do parasympathetic (vagal/pelvic) preganglionic fibres synapse?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: In the enteric plexuses (the ganglia in the gut wall) — so the preganglionic fibres are long and postganglionic fibres short.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Name the largest prevertebral plexus and what it surrounds.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: The coeliac plexus (with its coeliac ganglia), around the coeliac trunk — the foregut plexus.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Name the two plexuses of the enteric nervous system and their functions.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: The submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus — secretion & local blood flow; the myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus — motility/peristalsis.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What is Hirschsprung's disease?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Congenital absence of the myenteric & submucosal ganglia in a segment of bowel → a tonically contracted aganglionic segment and functional obstruction.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Which afferents carry foregut pain, and where is it referred?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: The greater splanchnic (T5–T9); referred to the epigastrium.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Which afferents carry midgut pain, and where is it referred?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: The lesser splanchnic (T10–T11); referred to the periumbilical (T10) region.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Which afferents carry hindgut pain, and where is it referred?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: The lumbar splanchnic (T12–L2); referred to the suprapubic / hypogastric region.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Explain the shift of pain in appendicitis.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Early periumbilical (T10, midgut visceral) pain from the inflamed appendix, then localisation to the right iliac fossa (McBurney’s point) as the parietal peritoneum is irritated (somatic).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What is a coeliac plexus block used for?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: To relieve the intractable pain of pancreatic cancer (and other foregut malignancies) by interrupting the foregut visceral afferents.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What is meralgia paraesthetica?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Entrapment of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh beneath the inguinal ligament → burning pain/numbness over the lateral thigh.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Why can a psoas abscess affect the lower limb nerves?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: The lumbar plexus lies within psoas major, so a psoas abscess/haematoma can compress the plexus (classically the femoral nerve).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Which reflex is lost with genitofemoral (genital branch) injury?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: The cremasteric reflex (its genital branch supplies the cremaster muscle).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Why do the splanchnic nerves matter for referred pain as well as sympathetic supply?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: They also carry the visceral pain afferents from the gut back to the spinal cord — the anatomical basis of referred abdominal pain.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Along what do the sympathetic postganglionic fibres travel to reach the gut?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Along the arteries (peri-arterial plexuses) — e.g. around the coeliac, superior & inferior mesenteric arteries.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: The transpyloric plane lies at which vertebral level?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: The transpyloric plane of Addison lies at L1, midway between the xiphisternum and umbilicus, crossing the pylorus, pancreatic neck, SMA origin and renal hila.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: The two layers of superficial fascia below the umbilicus are:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: Below the umbilicus the superficial fascia splits into Camper's (fatty, superficial) and Scarpa's (membranous, deep).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: The fibres of the external oblique muscle run:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: External oblique fibres pass inferomedially ('hands in pockets'); internal oblique runs at right angles (superomedial) and transversus abdominis is horizontal.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: Below the arcuate line, the posterior wall of the rectus sheath is formed by:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: Below the arcuate line all three aponeuroses pass anterior to rectus abdominis, leaving only transversalis fascia posteriorly — a relative weak point.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: The deep inguinal ring lies in the transversalis fascia, in what relation to the inferior epigastric vessels?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: The deep ring lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; an indirect hernia therefore enters lateral to these vessels.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: The inguinal ligament runs between which two bony points?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: The inguinal ligament is the rolled lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis, running from the ASIS to the pubic tubercle.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: An indirect inguinal hernia passes through the deep ring, which is located:
options: Medial to the inferior epigastric vessels
Lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: An indirect hernia enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels (congenital, via a patent processus vaginalis); a direct hernia is medial (Hesselbach's triangle).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: A direct inguinal hernia protrudes through:
options: Hesselbach's (inguinal) triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels
The superficial ring only, lateral to the vessels
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: A direct hernia pushes through the weakened posterior wall in Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: Which is the medial boundary of Hesselbach's triangle?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: Hesselbach's triangle is bounded medially by the lateral border of rectus abdominis, laterally by the inferior epigastric vessels, and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: A hernia located BELOW and LATERAL to the pubic tubercle is most likely a:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: A hernia below and lateral to the pubic tubercle is femoral; an inguinal hernia lies above and medial to the tubercle.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: Which of the following is a covering of the spermatic cord derived from internal oblique?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: The cremasteric fascia (and cremaster muscle) derive from internal oblique; the external spermatic fascia is from external oblique and the internal spermatic fascia from transversalis fascia.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: Which structure lies ON the spermatic cord rather than within it?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: The ilioinguinal nerve pierces internal oblique to enter the canal, lies on the cord (not within its coverings), and exits through the superficial ring.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: The anterior abdominal wall muscles are innervated by the anterior rami of:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: The thoraco-abdominal nerves (T7–T11), the subcostal (T12) and iliohypogastric/ilioinguinal (L1) supply the anterior abdominal wall.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: The median umbilical fold contains the remnant of the:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: The median umbilical fold overlies the urachus (median umbilical ligament); the medial folds contain the obliterated umbilical arteries and the lateral folds the inferior epigastric vessels.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: McBurney's point, overlying the appendix base, is located:
options: Halfway between the ASIS and pubic tubercle
One-third from the ASIS to the umbilicus
One-third from the umbilicus to the ASIS
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: McBurney's point is one-third of the way along a line from the ASIS to the umbilicus.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: A rectus sheath haematoma typically results from injury to the:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: Tearing of the inferior epigastric vessels (especially below the arcuate line, where they are unsupported posteriorly) produces a rectus sheath haematoma that can mimic an acute abdomen.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: Dilated para-umbilical veins ('caput medusae') indicate:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: Caput medusae results from portosystemic anastomosis at the umbilicus in portal hypertension, via recanalised para-umbilical veins.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: The chief flexor of the hip, formed by psoas major and iliacus, is the:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: Psoas major and iliacus unite as iliopsoas, inserting on the lesser trochanter — the principal hip flexor; a psoas abscess can track to the groin.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: Early appendicitis produces peri-umbilical pain because the umbilicus is the ____ dermatome.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: The umbilicus is the T10 dermatome; early visceral appendiceal pain is referred here before localising to the right iliac fossa.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: Which vessel supplies the foregut, and to what surface region is foregut pain referred?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The foregut is supplied by the coeliac trunk (T12); its visceral pain is referred to the epigastrium.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: Midgut structures are supplied by the SMA and refer pain to the:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The midgut (SMA, L1) refers pain to the periumbilical region — the basis of early appendicitis pain.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: The foregut–midgut junction lies at which structure?
options: The 2nd part of the duodenum (major duodenal papilla)
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The foregut becomes the midgut at the 2nd part of the duodenum, at the major duodenal papilla where the bile and pancreatic ducts enter.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: Which of the following is NOT retroperitoneal?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The transverse colon is intraperitoneal (on the transverse mesocolon); the ascending/descending colon, duodenum (2nd/3rd), pancreas (except tail) and kidneys are retroperitoneal (SAD PUCKER).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: The left gastric artery, supplying the lesser curve of the stomach, arises from the:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The left gastric artery is a direct branch of the coeliac trunk; the right gastric arises from the hepatic artery.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: The major duodenal papilla (of Vater) is located in which part of the duodenum?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The major duodenal papilla, where the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct open, lies in the 2nd (descending) part of the duodenum.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: Which feature is characteristic of the ILEUM (versus the jejunum)?
options: Peyer's patches and numerous arterial arcades
Location in the upper left abdomen
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The ileum has abundant Peyer's patches and many short arterial arcades; the jejunum has taller plicae circulares, a thicker wall and long vasa recta.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: A Meckel's diverticulum is classically found how far from the ileocaecal valve?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The 'rule of 2s': ~2% of people, ~2 feet from the ileocaecal valve, ~2 inches long, often 2 tissue types (ectopic gastric/pancreatic mucosa).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: The three teniae coli converge at the base of which structure?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The teniae coli converge on the base of the appendix — a useful surgical landmark for locating it.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: The splenic flexure is a watershed area vulnerable to ischaemia because it lies between the:
options: Left and right colic arteries only
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The splenic flexure is the border between the SMA (midgut) and IMA (hindgut) territories, linked only by the marginal artery — hence a watershed for ischaemic colitis.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: The portal triad within the porta hepatis consists of the:
options: Portal vein, IVC and bile duct
Portal vein, hepatic artery and common hepatic duct
Hepatic vein, hepatic artery and bile duct
Portal vein, hepatic artery and hepatic vein
Aorta, portal vein and bile duct
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The porta hepatis transmits the portal vein, hepatic artery (proper) and the common hepatic/bile duct — the portal triad.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: Calot's (cystohepatic) triangle contains which artery, important in cholecystectomy?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: Calot's triangle (cystic duct, common hepatic duct, inferior liver edge) contains the cystic artery, which must be identified and ligated during cholecystectomy.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: The common bile duct joins the main pancreatic duct at the:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The common bile duct and main pancreatic duct unite at the ampulla of Vater, guarded by the sphincter of Oddi, opening at the major duodenal papilla.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: The tail of the pancreas is unusual among pancreatic parts because it is:
options: Intraperitoneal (in the splenorenal ligament, reaching the splenic hilum)
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The tail of the pancreas is intraperitoneal, lying in the splenorenal ligament and reaching the splenic hilum; the rest of the pancreas is retroperitoneal.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: The spleen lies deep to which ribs?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The spleen lies in the left hypochondrium along ribs 9–11 and can be ruptured by fractures of the left lower ribs.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: At the renal hilum, the order of structures from anterior to posterior is:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: From front to back the renal hilum transmits the renal vein, then the artery, then the ureter (renal pelvis) — 'VAU'.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: The right kidney lies lower than the left because it is displaced by the:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The right kidney is pushed inferiorly by the large right lobe of the liver, so it sits lower than the left.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: The left suprarenal (adrenal) vein drains into the:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The left adrenal vein drains into the left renal vein; the right adrenal vein drains directly into the IVC.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: A posterior ulcer in the first part of the duodenum characteristically erodes which artery?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The gastroduodenal artery lies immediately behind the first part of the duodenum; a posterior D1 ulcer can erode it, causing major upper-GI haemorrhage.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.question: Rupture of the spleen classically causes referred pain to the left shoulder tip, known as:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs.explanation: Kehr's sign is left shoulder-tip pain from diaphragmatic (phrenic C3–5) irritation by blood after splenic rupture.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: The lumbar plexus is formed within which muscle?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The lumbar plexus (L1–L4) is formed within the substance of the psoas major muscle.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: Which nerve emerges from the LATERAL border of psoas major?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The femoral nerve (and lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh) emerge from the lateral border of psoas; the obturator emerges medially and the genitofemoral pierces its anterior surface.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies which muscle?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremaster muscle (and mediates the cremasteric reflex); the femoral branch is purely sensory.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: Which nerve, when entrapped under the inguinal ligament, causes meralgia paraesthetica?
options: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: Meralgia paraesthetica is entrapment of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (L2–L3), causing burning pain/numbness over the lateral thigh.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: The greater splanchnic nerve (T5–T9) synapses in which ganglion?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The greater splanchnic nerve synapses in the coeliac ganglion and supplies the foregut.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: What is characteristic of the thoracic and lumbar splanchnic nerves at the sympathetic chain?
options: They synapse in the chain ganglia
They are preganglionic fibres that pass through the chain without synapsing
They carry only motor fibres to skeletal muscle
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The splanchnic nerves are preganglionic sympathetic fibres that pass through the sympathetic chain without synapsing, synapsing instead in the pre-aortic ganglia.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: The vagus nerve supplies the gut parasympathetically as far as the:
options: Distal third of the transverse colon
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The vagus supplies the foregut and midgut, reaching the distal third of the transverse colon; the hindgut beyond this is supplied by the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–4).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: Sympathetic stimulation of the gut characteristically causes:
options: Decreased motility, sphincter contraction and vasoconstriction
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: Sympathetic activity decreases gut motility and secretion, contracts sphincters and causes vasoconstriction; parasympathetic activity does the opposite.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: Which enteric plexus principally controls gut motility (peristalsis)?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus, lying between the muscle layers, controls motility; the submucosal (Meissner's) plexus controls secretion and local blood flow.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: Hirschsprung's disease results from congenital absence of the:
options: Enteric (myenteric and submucosal) ganglia in a bowel segment
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: Hirschsprung's disease is congenital aganglionosis (absent myenteric and submucosal ganglia), producing a tonically contracted segment and functional obstruction.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: Early appendicitis pain is felt periumbilically because the appendix is a ____ structure whose visceral afferents enter the cord at ____.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The appendix is a midgut structure; its visceral pain afferents enter the cord around T10, referring pain to the periumbilical region before it localises to the RIF.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: Foregut visceral pain is referred to which region?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: Foregut pain (afferents with the greater splanchnic, T5–T9) is referred to the epigastrium.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: A coeliac plexus block is most useful for the pain of:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: A coeliac plexus block interrupts foregut visceral afferents and is used to relieve the intractable pain of pancreatic (and other upper-GI) cancer.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: Which nerves supply the hindgut with parasympathetic fibres?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The hindgut (distal third of transverse colon onward) receives parasympathetic supply from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–4); the vagus supplies foregut and midgut.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: The lesser splanchnic nerve arises from which roots?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The lesser splanchnic nerve arises from T10–T11 and synapses in the aorticorenal/superior mesenteric ganglion, supplying the midgut.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: A psoas abscess may compress which nerve, given the plexus lies within psoas?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: Because the lumbar plexus lies within psoas major, a psoas abscess or haematoma classically compresses the femoral nerve.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: Postganglionic sympathetic fibres reach the abdominal viscera by travelling along the:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: Postganglionic sympathetic fibres from the pre-aortic ganglia travel along the branches of the aorta (peri-arterial plexuses) to reach the gut.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: The ilioinguinal nerve arises from which root?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The ilioinguinal nerve arises from L1 (as does the iliohypogastric) and runs through the inguinal canal to supply the upper medial thigh and anterior scrotum/labium.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.question: Hindgut visceral pain afferents travel with the lumbar splanchnic nerves and refer pain to the:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: Hindgut pain (afferents with the lumbar splanchnic nerves, T12–L2) is referred to the suprapubic/hypogastric region.
